title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration employed shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Important methodological caveat (explicit): because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We explicitly document artifact evidence that rules out prompt/response contamination in representative provider calls, explain why the repair subsystem was not invoked (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces), and provide the archived manifests and per‑task validator traces that support all claims. The preregistered hypotheses about generator/repair superiority (H1/H2) remain preregistered but unobserved under the shared_initial_candidate execution semantics.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both deterministic correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two architectural approaches are commonly proposed: (A) translation‑first pipelines that restrict generation to a vendor DSL and apply formal verification/solver feedback, and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair.

This study preregistered a head‑to‑head, paired design to answer: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation: reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed N = 120 paired tasks, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and the analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1. Crucially, the preregistration specified shared_initial_candidate semantics: each paired task used a single LLM generation and that identical candidate was supplied to both downstream arms. We emphasize this design decision: the confirmatory estimand tested here is validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates, not independent generator or repair efficacy. The Methods and Results below incorporate artifact references that demonstrate (1) the orchestration and provider accounting consistent with one shared generation per pair, (2) provider_call traces that show prompts did not contain canonical reference answers for representative tasks, and (3) per‑task validator traces that explain why repairs were never invoked.
sections.related_work: Prior work falls into two methodological families relevant to our axes: (1) translation and formal verification systems (DSL synthesis + solver verification) that prioritize deterministic guarantees and low generator variance [10,11,5], and (2) LLM‑driven agentic NetOps approaches that emphasize flexible natural‑language→CLI mapping and iterative repair, often evaluating generator sampling and repair coverage [3,4]. Translation‑first systems focus on solver scalability and counterexample diagnostics; LLM‑centric studies focus on sample variance, repair traces, and transient unsafe‑proposal rates. Recent instrumented pipelines combine deterministic validators with multi‑agent repair loops to reduce hallucination; these works differ in whether generator outputs are sampled independently per arm or held fixed to test downstream orchestration differences. Our run purposely adopts the latter to isolate validator acceptance for identical candidates. Representative verified references used for positioning include canonical network verification and recent LLM‑for‑NetOps studies (cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and execution contract. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) froze the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), shared_initial_candidate semantics, maximum_model_calls = 240, and analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1. The preregistration and execution manifest are archived as part of the artifact bundle referenced throughout.

Task generation and canonical references. Confirmatory tasks (120 pairs) were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each manifest entry includes: intent text, canonical reference answer (normalized_reference_answer), initial and expected final states, and a required_sequence. Representative manifest entries and their canonical reference answers are archived (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative task entries such as pair‑000001 in the archived bundle).

Generation semantics, provider accounting, and isolation. The orchestration implemented shared_initial_candidate: one LLM call per pair whose textual candidate was delivered identically to both downstream arms. Execution accounting in the manifest records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120. Deterministic reconciliation shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). These artifacts together demonstrate that the system performed exactly one independent generation per pair and maintained execution isolation consistent with the preregistration.

Prompt contamination check (required revision). To address concerns that the generator prompt may have admitted the canonical reference and thereby produced trivial matches, representative provider_call traces were inspected. For example, the execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json artifact references the shared initial provider trace at execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json (sha256 recorded in the scoring JSON). The provider_call trace files in execution/provider_calls/ (representative paths recorded in per‑task scoring JSONs) contain the exact request metadata and the prompt content sent to the hosted model for the shared generation. Inspection of these archived provider_call files confirms the prompt consisted of the task intent, constraint fields, and generation instructions (no canonical reference_answer field was injected into the prompt). The per‑task scoring JSONs explicitly link to the provider_call trace paths and their SHA‑256 values (e.g., task‑000001 shared_initial_provider_trace_sha256 = 3ead014b33...), enabling verification that the canonical reference was not echoed into the model prompt; readers can audit the archived provider_call JSONs at the listed paths to confirm the same fact. (The per‑task scoring JSONs and their provider_call path fields are archived in execution/scoring/ and execution/provider_calls/ as part of the submission bundle.)

Deterministic validator rules and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executes full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency, and returns validation_after.valid (boolean). A task is scored success (1) only when validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_response, repair_applied flags, and pointers to provider_call traces; these files are the canonical evidence for per‑task decisions.
sections.results:
Execution and provider accounting. The execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared LLM call per pair). Deterministic reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms complete_pair_count = 120 and provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 120, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false. These artifacts substantiate the single shared generation per pair.

Primary contingency and statistics. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0; paired difference A − B = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.00, 0.00] and exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) and reproducible via paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Why repairs were not invoked (required revision). Across all per‑task scoring JSONs the archived fields show repair_applied = false and repair_provider_trace_path = null. Representative examples illustrate the pattern: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json records parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validation_after.valid = true, and repair_applied = false; task‑000002 shows parsed_command_count = 2 and required_command_count = 2 with validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false; task‑000003 shows parsed_command_count = 6 and required_command_count = 6 with validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false. Because the shared_initial_candidate fulfilled the validator's required_command_count and ordering/dependency checks in these examples, the repair subsystem was not triggered. The repair subsystem remained enabled by design (the orchestration code records repair_provider_trace_path fields when invoked), but all per‑task traces show null repair_provider_trace_path and repair_applied=false, demonstrating archival evidence that repair was live but uninvoked for every episode.

Contamination and missingness diagnostics. The contamination summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) is empty (no flags). The missingness summary (analysis/missingness_summary.csv) reports complete_pairs = 120 and zeros for all missingness counters. Provider audit logs and execution traces show no model‑call failures beyond the planned single generation per pair. These artifacts are available for inspection in the archived bundle.

Observed estimand vs preregistered hypotheses. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics were used, the measured estimand is validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates; the preregistered hypotheses H1 and H2 about comparative end‑to‑end success rates and repair coverage under independent generation sampling remain preregistered but unobserved in this execution. The analysis artifacts and preregistration record this design choice and its consequences explicitly.
sections.discussion:
What we measured and its operational meaning. The run provides artifact‑grounded evidence that, given identical LLM candidates, translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair orchestration paths produced identical deterministic validator acceptance outcomes under the chosen emulator, task corpus, and validator (n11 = 120). This is a narrow but operationally useful property: validator‑acceptance parity implies that swapping downstream orchestration or verification layers will not change acceptance for identical proposals under the given validator semantics.

What we did not measure. Because the generator draw was shared, generator sampling variance, independent repair coverage, transient unsafe proposals produced only when arms generate separately, and multi‑model generality were not exercised. The preregistration anticipated these secondary estimands (repair coverage, mean repair iterations) but their measurement requires nonzero repair_applied events and independent-generation semantics; neither occurred here. The archived artifacts explicitly show repair_applied = false for all episodes, so the preregistered secondary tests are unobserved rather than falsified.

Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of concordance. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs show normalized_response frequently matched the canonical reference modulo trivial ordering differences; parsed_command_count equaled required_command_count in the representative examples, producing validation_after.valid = true and avoiding repair. These per‑task fields provide a mechanistic account (and archival evidence) of why repair remained unnecessary.

Design implications and concrete next steps. To test the originally preregistered H1/H2 about independent generation and repair efficacy the protocol must be modified in reproducible ways that leave an artifact trail: (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent LLM generation per pair (this increases initial model_calls_used from 120 to 240); (ii) enable independent sampling or multiple initial candidates per arm to estimate generator variance; (iii) instrument and allow repair iterations (repair_provider_trace_path nonnull and repair_applied true for some episodes) to observe repair_coverage and mean repair iterations; (iv) optionally increase emulator fidelity or include hardware checks to reduce simulator/hardware divergence risk. Each change would be visible in the execution artifacts (higher hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_provider_trace paths, nondegenerate contingency tables) and hence reproducible.

Threats to validity (artifact‑anchored). Internal validity: shared_candidate semantics intentionally removed generator variance and thus narrowed the estimand; this is a preregistered design choice rather than an unplanned confound (preregistration and execution manifests archived). Construct validity: deterministic validator acceptance is a conservative gate that compresses multiple operator concerns into a single pass/fail signal; per‑task parsed counts and violation codes in scoring JSONs are archived for graded analyses. External validity: the synthetic Mininet‑derived task corpus, single model (gpt‑5‑mini), and single validator limit generality; these constraints are explicit in the preregistration and manifest. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency (all concordant) yields a point mass CI and p = 1.0; analysis artifacts (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, paired_contingency_table.csv) document the exact computation and seeds.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifactized paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). Repairs were not applied in any episode (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces), so preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved. The archived manifests, provider_call traces, and per‑task scoring JSONs support all claims and permit independent audit: provider_call traces show prompts contained only task intents and constraints (no canonical reference answers), and scoring traces show parsed_command_count == required_command_count in representative examples that led to validator acceptance. Future confirmatory experiments to test generator and repair hypotheses should adopt independent per‑arm generation, increase model_call budgets, and enable repair instrumentation; these modifications are explicitly documented in the preregistration as reproducible changes.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures (H1/H2 remained preregistered but unobserved under these semantics).

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
